{{short description|Species of plant}} {{Speciesbox | image = Leycesteria formosa.jpg | genus = Leycesteria | species = formosa | authority = [[Nathaniel Wallich|Wall.]] }} '''''Leycesteria formosa''''', the '''pheasant berry''',{{BSBI 2007 |accessdate=2014-10-17 }} is a deciduous shrub in the family [[Caprifoliaceae]], native to the [[Himalayas]] and southwestern [[China]]. It is considered a noxious [[invasive species]] in Australia, New Zealand, the neighbouring islands of Micronesia, and some other places.{{Cite web|url=http://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/10061/Leycesteria-formosa/Details|title=Leycesteria formosa | Himalayan honeysuckle/RHS Gardening|website=www.rhs.org.uk|access-date=2021-07-03|archive-date=2021-07-11|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210711074150/https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/10061/Leycesteria-formosa/Details|url-status=live}}Silva, L., E. Ojeda Land & J.L. Rodríguez Luengo (eds.) 2008. Invasive terrestrial flora and fauna of Macaronesia. Top 100 in Azores, Madeira and Canaries. ARENA, Ponta Delgada. 546 p{{cite journal |last1=Silva |first1=Luís |last2=Marcelino |first2=José |last3=Resendes |first3=Roberto |last4=Moniz |first4=João |title=First record of the top invasive plant ''Leycesteria formosa'' (Caprifoliacea) in Terceira Island, Azores |journal=Arquipélago – Life and Marine Sciences |date=2009 |volume=26 |pages=69–72 |hdl=10400.3/452 |url=http://www.okeanos.uac.pt/storage/2009/02/pp_69-72_Silva_etal_26.pdf }} In the Himalayas, the shrub is frequently used in the traditional medicine of the various countries and peoples encompassed within the region. == Names == The genus name ''Leycesteria'' was coined by [[Nathaniel Wallich]] (one time director of [[Acharya Jagadish Chandra Bose Indian Botanic Garden|Royal Botanic Garden, Calcutta]]) in honour of his friend William Leycester, [[Chief justice]] and noted amateur [[horticulturist]], in [[Bengal]] in about 1820;The Names of Plants, D. Gledhill, Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, Uk. rep. 1994. {{ISBN|0521366755}}. p128 while the [[Latin]] specific name ''formosa'' (feminine form of ''formosus'') signifies 'beautiful' or 'handsome' (literally: 'shapely'){{APNI | name = ''Lambertia formosa'' | id =62432 |accessdate=3 March 2013}}{{cite book |author1=Knight, Joseph |author2=[Salisbury, Richard] | year = 1809 | title = On the Cultivation of the Plants Belonging to the Natural Order of Proteeae | publisher = W. Savage |location= London, United Kingdom |page = 109|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=dkUAAAAAQAAJ&q=Persoonia}} – in reference to the curious, pendent [[inflorescence]]s with their richly wine-coloured [[bract]]s. There is a popular misconception, however, that the specific name derives from the place name 'Formosa', which is an abbreviation of the original [[Portuguese language|Portuguese]] name for the island of [[Taiwan]]: ''Ilha Formosa'' "beautiful island".{{cite book |chapter=Chapter 3: History |chapter-url=http://www.gio.gov.tw/taiwan-website/5-gp/yearbook/docs/ch03.pdf |title=The Republic of China Yearbook 2011 |year=2011 |publisher=Government Information Office, Republic of China (Taiwan) |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120514004941/http://www.gio.gov.tw/taiwan-website/5-gp/yearbook/docs/ch03.pdf |archive-date=14 May 2012 |page=46}}. Portuguese is a [[romance language]] (i.e. derived from Latin) and the adjective ''formosa'' has passed into it unchanged in spelling and meaning from the original Latin. ''Leycesteria formosa'' is so named in recognition of its beauty, not in acknowledgment of an origin on the island now known as Taiwan.{{Citation |title=Formosa |date=2023-08-21 |url=https://en.wiktionary.org/w/index.php?title=Formosa&oldid=75740452 |work=Wiktionary, the free dictionary |access-date=2023-08-29 |language=en}}{{Citation |title=formosus |date=2023-01-13 |url=https://en.wiktionary.org/w/index.php?title=formosus&oldid=70818911 |work=Wiktionary, the free dictionary |access-date=2023-08-29 |language=en}} The Latin specific names of certain plants, given to indicate that they were native to Taiwan at a time when it was known as Formosa take such forms as ''formosae'', ''formosana'' and ''formosensis'', not the Latin adjective/Portuguese adjective-used-as-a-proper-noun ''formosa''.{{Cite web |title=提議修改維也納版國際命名法規53.3條款?證9 |url=https://9lib.co/document/9yn2wj0y-%E6%8F%90%E8%AD%B0%E4%BF%AE%E6%94%B9%E7%B6%AD%E4%B9%9F%E7%B4%8D%E7%89%88%E5%9C%8B%E9%9A%9B%E5%91%BD%E5%90%8D%E6%B3%95%E8%A6%8F533%E6%A2%9D%E6%AC%BE%E8%AD%899.html |access-date=2023-08-29 |website=9lib.co |language=tw |archive-date=2023-04-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230426012222/https://9lib.co/document/9yn2wj0y-%E6%8F%90%E8%AD%B0%E4%BF%AE%E6%94%B9%E7%B6%AD%E4%B9%9F%E7%B4%8D%E7%89%88%E5%9C%8B%E9%9A%9B%E5%91%BD%E5%90%8D%E6%B3%95%E8%A6%8F533%E6%A2%9D%E6%AC%BE%E8%AD%899.html |url-status=live }} Other common names include '''Himalayan honeysuckle''', '''pheasant-eye''', '''[[Elisha]]'s tears''', '''flowering nutmeg''', '''spiderwort''', '''Cape fuchsia''', '''whistle stick''', '''Himalaya nutmeg''', '''granny's curls''',{{Cite web |title=Leycesteria formosa - ''Excursion Flora of the British Isles''. Cambridge University Press. {{ISBN|0-521-04656-4}} Contrary to the impression given by the respective common names, the plant is completely unrelated either to the [[Myristica fragrans|nutmeg tree]] or to the [[fuchsia]]. Further contrary to the name "[[Cape Colony|Cape]] fuchsia", it is not native to South Africa – the name being especially inappropriate, given that the family Caprifoliaceae as a whole is absent from [[Sub-Saharan Africa]].{{cite journal |last1=Bell |first1=C. D. |last2=Donoghue |first2=M. J. |title=Dating the Dipsacales: comparing models, genes, and evolutionary implications |journal=American Journal of Botany |date=1 February 2005 |volume=92 |issue=2 |pages=284–296 |doi=10.3732/ajb.92.2.284|pmid=21652406 |doi-access=free }}
Wallich was Danish by birth and perhaps could hardly be expected to forsee that within fifty years or so the name of the worthy Justice [Leycester(ia)] would be corrupted into 'Elisha's tears' – which yet seems strangely to suit the plant, with its pendent white flowers and its persistent bracts which darken to a sombre blood red as the season advances.

''Garden Shrubs and their Histories''
[[Alice M. Coats]]Coats, Alice M. ''Garden Shrubs and their Histories'' pub. Vista Books, Longacre Press Ltd., 161-166 Fleet st., London E.C.4., 1963, entry ''Leycesteria'' pps. 195-197.
It is apparent from the above that the common name ''Elisha's tears'' falls into the same category (of jocular corruptions of the scientific names of plants into common names more congenial to rural British taste) as ''Aunt Eliza'' (for [[Crocosmia paniculata|Antholyza]]){{Cite web |title=Crocosmia paniculata |url=https://www.shootgardening.com/plants/crocosmia-paniculata |access-date=2023-08-29 |website=www.shootgardening.com |archive-date=2023-08-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230829083112/https://www.shootgardening.com/plants/crocosmia-paniculata |url-status=live }}{{cite web|url=http://www.theafricangarden.com/crocosmia_paniculata.html|title=Crocosmia paniculata - Aunt Liza|work=The African Garden|accessdate=4 September 2012}}{{Dead link|date=September 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} and ''Sally-my-handsome'' for [[Mesembryanthemum]].{{Cite web |title=Seasonal Wild Flowers - Sally-my-handsome |url=http://www.seasonalwildflowers.com/sally-my-handsome.html |access-date=2023-08-29 |website=www.seasonalwildflowers.com |archive-date=2023-05-28 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230528193524/http://www.seasonalwildflowers.com/sally-my-handsome.html |url-status=live }} It is also testament to a greater familiarity with the names of biblical figures – such as the Old Testament prophets – on the part of Britons of the nineteenth century, when compared to their counterparts in the twenty-first.{{cite journal |last1=Field |first1=Clive D. |title=Is the Bible Becoming a Closed Book? British Opinion Poll Evidence |journal=Journal of Contemporary Religion |date=2 September 2014 |volume=29 |issue=3 |pages=503–528 |doi=10.1080/13537903.2014.945735|s2cid=143654509 |doi-access=free }} == Affiliation within Caprifoliaceae == The results of the genetic testing undertaken by Zhang et al. have revealed that Leycesteria is most closely related to the genera ''[[Triosteum]]'' (common name – "horse gentians"; Chinese: 莛子藨属; tíng zi biāo shǔ) and ''[[Heptacodium]]'' (Chinese common name: 七子花; qī zi huā; lit. "seven son flower"). Of these, only ''Triosteum'' has fruits that are berries, the fruits of ''Heptacodium'' being dry capsules.{{cite journal |last1=Zhang |first1=Haizhu |title=Characterization of the complete chloroplast genome of ''Leycesteria formosa'' wall. (Caprifoliaceae), a medicinal plant in southwest China |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/338533120 |journal=Mitochondrial DNA Part B |date=2 January 2020 |volume=5 |issue=1 |pages=500–501 |doi=10.1080/23802359.2019.1704652|pmid=33366620 |pmc=7748767 }} These three genera belong to the subfamily Caprifolioideae of the honeysuckle family Caprifoliaceae, the other two genera in the subfamily being ''[[Lonicera]]'', the (true) honeysuckles and ''[[Symphoricarpos]]'', the snowberries.{{Cite web | url=http://www.mobot.org/MOBOT/research/APweb/welcome.html | title=Angiosperm Phylogeny Website | access-date=2021-11-11 | archive-date=2010-02-06 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100206221914/http://www.mobot.org/mobot/research/apweb/welcome.html | url-status=live }} == Description ==
It is found to be a hardy evergreen, requiring a considerable degree of moisture, and a situation slightly sheltered and shaded, though the colour of its bracts would be most probably be heightened by exposure to solar light. Propagation is effected by cuttings or layers.
[[Joseph Paxton]]
''Paxton's Magazine of Botany'' Volume VI (1839) ''Paxton's Magazine of Botany'', Volume 6, pub. London 1839 by W.S. Orr and Co. Paternoster Row
A deciduous, sometimes evergreen, half-woody, shrub-like plant (intermediate between a shrub and a herbaceous perennial) with young stems that are soft, hollow and upright in various shades of green, salmon pink, maroon and purple, {{convert|1–3|m|abbr=on}}https://www.devonpondplants.co.uk/product/leycesteria-formosa-himalayan-honeysuckle/ {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211201112038/https://www.devonpondplants.co.uk/product/leycesteria-formosa-himalayan-honeysuckle/ |date=2021-12-01 }} Retrieved at 11.19 on Wed 1/12/21. in height, which may only last for 2–5 years before collapsing and being replaced by new stems from the roots. Mature specimens, however, may have short, truly woody trunks clothed in rough, grey bark at the base. The [[leaf|leaves]] are opposite, dark green and usually cordate {{convert|6–18|cm|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|4–9|cm|abbr=on}} broad, with an entire, wavy or even deeply lobed margin and often an extended [[Glossary of botanical terms#D|drip tip]] (commonly an adaptation to a wet climate). The [[flower]]s (bee-pollinatedPhillips, Roger and Rix, Martyn, ''The Botanical Garden:'', pub. Macmillan 2002, vol. 1 ''Trees and Shrubs: a photographic record of the genera of trees and shrubs of interest to gardeners'' p.445.) are produced on {{convert|5–10|cm|abbr=on}} long pendulous [[raceme]]s; each flower is small, white, pale pink or rarely deep purplish pink, subtended by a purplish-pink bract, terminating – like the leaves – in a drip tip. The [[fruit]] is a [[Berry (botany)|berry]], hard and deep pink when unripe, and fragile, soft (easily burst) and a deep purple-brown when ripe and measuring 1 cm in diameter.Online flora of China http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200022271 {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211207154127/http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200022271 |date=2021-12-07 }} Retrieved at 18.16 on Tuesday 16/11/21. The berries are eaten avidly by birds, which disperse the seeds in their droppings.[[Polunin, Oleg]] and Stainton, Adam, ''Flowers of the Himalaya'', pub. Oxford University Press 1984, p.165 species no. 583. The berries are unpleasantly bitter when unripe, but, once soft and deep purple-brown in colour, are edible and sweet, having a mild flavour reminiscent of [[toffee]] or [[caramel]]. Being a recent introduction to Europe, the plant lacks any traditional uses there.[https://web.archive.org/web/20130725145047/http://fergustheforager.co.uk/recipes-articles/himalayan-honeysuckle/ Himalayan honeysuckle], Fergus The Forager[https://www.wildfooduk.com/edible-wild-plants/pheasant-berry/ Pheasant Berry], Wild Food UK == Distribution ==
''L. formosa'' includes within its wide range of distribution the areas of all the other known species of the genus. From the [[North-West Frontier Province]] and the [[Punjab]] it ranges the whole length of the Himalaya eastwards to south-eastern Yunnan, where it was collected by Henry near [[Mengzi City|Mengtze]], and north-eastwards to Szechuan and eastern Tibet, where [[Alfred Rehder|Rehder]]'s var. ''stenosepala'' appears to replace very largely the typical form.
''A Revision of the Genus Leycesteria''
— [[Herbert Kenneth Airy Shaw|H.K. Airy-Shaw]]Airy-Shaw, H.K., "A revision of the genus Leycesteria" ''Bulletin of Miscellaneous Information Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew'' No. 4 1932, XXI
The species is native to Pakistan, India, Nepal, East and West Himalaya, Southwestern China (Sichuan, Yunnan and Guizhou), Tibet and Myanmar.Kew Plants of the World Online http://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:148526-1 {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211101181449/http://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:148526-1 |date=2021-11-01 }} Retrieved at 18.12 on Monday 1/11/21. == Introduction to the U.K. == Coats notes that according to [[John Claudius Loudon]]''Arboretum et fruticetum Britannicum; or, The trees and shrubs of Britain'' [[John Claudius Loudon]] the plant was brought into cultivation in 1824 and flowered soon afterwards in Allen and Rogers's Bolingbroke Nursery in [[Battersea]]; and that it was grown at about the same time in the gardens of the [[Royal Horticultural Society]] (known at that time as the Horticultural Society of London) from seed procured from India by [[John Forbes Royle]]. It proved something of a disappointment to those whose expectations had been raised by a rather highly coloured plate of it in Wallich's ''Plantae Asiaticae Rariores'' (1830-2) [see image of said plate in gallery below].
Its leaves are a pale dull green...it has a rambling inelegant mode of growth, and the colour of the bracts is not at all brighter than what is represented in the accompanying plate.
[[John Lindley]]
[[The Botanical Register]] (1839)[[John Lindley]], [[The Botanical Register]] (1839)
The character of the plant, as developed in an artificial climate, is far from being so good as the accounts of Indian botanists had led us to anticipate. The foliage is large and handsome, and the flowers appear to be produced numerously in terminal pendent racemes; but the most showy feature is the large bracteae at the base of the flowers, which are beautifully veined and tipped with crimson. Dr. Lindley suggests that this latter character may be more prominently exhibited as the plant becomes older, and more inured to our system of cultivation.
[[Joseph Paxton]]
''Paxton's Magazine of Botany'' Volume VI (1839)
''L. formosa'' was expected, at the time of its introduction, to be frost-tender in the UK and therefore to need a sunny, South or West-facing aspect, but was soon found to prefer, on the contrary, a cool position, being a plant of dappled woodland shade. Rallying after his initial disappointment, Lindley could concede
If grown in the shade it is most likely to be a beautiful object.
and, a century or so later, Coats could give it similarly mixed praise, prescient in her anticipation of the plant's subsequent classification, in certain other countries, as an invasive weed:
Its hardiness and ease of propagation have led to it being regarded as a background-shrub, and its peculiar merits are rather overlooked. The design of its hanging racemes is unusual and striking.
''Leycesteria formosa'' became a popular plant in [[Victorian era|Victorian]] shrubberies, grown because the berries were relished by the [[pheasant]]s raised as game birds on country estates – whence the English common name ''pheasant berry''.Bean, W. ''Trees and Shrubs Hardy in Great Britain'', pub. Murray 1981.Thomas, G.S. ''Ornamental Shrubs, Climbers and Bamboos'', pub. Murray 1992. ISBN 0-7195-5043-2. Attempts have been made in recent years to re-popularise the species in Britain, with new cultivated varieties appearing in garden centres.{{Cite web |last= |first= |date=2021-09-01 |title=Leycesteria 'Little Lanterns' {{!}} Himalayan Honeysuckle |url=https://mrplantgeek.com/2021/09/01/leycesteria-little-lanterns-himalayan-honeysuckle/ |access-date=2023-08-29 |website=Michael Perry - Mr Plant Geek |language=en-US |archive-date=2023-10-20 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231020234231/https://mrplantgeek.com/2021/09/01/leycesteria-little-lanterns-himalayan-honeysuckle/ |url-status=live }}https://www.gardenbeauty.co.uk/leycesteria-formosa {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211120000143/https://www.gardenbeauty.co.uk/leycesteria-formosa |date=2021-11-20 }} Retrieved at 00.00 on Saturday 20/11/21. == Habitat and cultivation == In the wild, in the eastern Himalayas and western China, the plant grows in wet, rocky woods and on cliffs, its predeliction for the latter habitat explaining its success in colonising walls – effectively artificial cliffs.{{Cite news |title=Plant This . . .? No, Don't |url=https://www.irishtimes.com/opinion/plant-this-no-don-t-1.209553 |access-date=2023-08-29 |newspaper=The Irish Times |language=en}} The plant was included in a list of species observed to be resistant to gross atmospheric [[pollution]] (smoke and other [[particulate]]s) compiled in the late 19th century.Hough, Franklin B. ''Report upon Forestry'', prepared under the direction of the Commissioner of Agriculture in pursuance of an act of Congress, approved August 15, 1876, pub. Washington government printing office 1878, Volume 1, section "Injurious effects of smoke, and of noxious gas(s)es upon trees" p. 182Hutchinson, Robert, of Carlowrie, Kirkliston, prize essay, "Effects produced on Trees and Shrubs by Smoke from Public Works", Transac. Highland and Ag. Soc., 1876, p.191. It is equally resistant to modern atmospheric pollution and will tolerate windy sites and the salty air of coastal localities.{{Cite web |last= |date=2020-05-24 |title=鬼吹簫 (Himalayan Honeysuckle) |url=https://blog.xuite.net/cshuang2/twblog/589151702 |access-date=2023-08-29 |website=隨意窩 Xuite日誌 |language=zh-TW |archive-date=2023-08-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230829083517/https://blog.xuite.net/cshuang2/twblog/589151702 |url-status=live }} Furthermore, deer will not browse upon it. It is often found naturalised in the wild in southern England.{{Cite web|title=British Wild Plant: Leycesteria formosa Himalayan Honeysuckle|url=https://www.ukwildflowers.com/Web_pages/leycesteria_formosa_himalayan_honeysuckle.htm|access-date=2020-06-16|website=www.ukwildflowers.com}} In [[Ireland]] it is found in roadsides, planted wooded areas, and riverbanks.Parnell, J. and Curtis, T. 2012 ''Webb's An Irish Flora''. Cork University Press.{{ISBN|978-185918-4783}} ==Medicinal uses== ''L. formosa'' is a frequently used medicinal plant in Southwest China, where it bears the common name ''Yi Yao''. The [[Yi people]] (known also as ''Nuoso'' and ''Lolo'') of [[Sichuan]] province use the tender shoots of the plant in their system of [[traditional medicine]] to treat [[measles]].{{cite journal |last1=Wang |first1=Jing |last2=Seyler |first2=Barnabas C. |last3=Ticktin |first3=Tamara |last4=Zeng |first4=Yonggang |last5=Ayu |first5=Kede |title=An ethnobotanical survey of wild edible plants used by the Yi people of Liangshan Prefecture, Sichuan Province, China |journal=Journal of Ethnobiology and Ethnomedicine |date=December 2020 |volume=16 |issue=1 |pages=10 |doi=10.1186/s13002-019-0349-5 |pmid=32102675 |pmc=7045740 |doi-access=free }} The Yi (speakers of various [[Loloish languages]] of [[Burmese language|Burmese]] affiliation{{cite web|url=https://www.rflr.org/linguistics/burmese-lolo/survey/|title=Research Foundation Language and Religion|date=|accessdate=2020-02-17|archive-date=2021-05-13|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210513003451/https://www.rflr.org/linguistics/burmese-lolo/survey/|url-status=live}}) are notable for their rich cultural heritage, having retained their ancient [[shamanism|shamanic]] faith of [[Bimoism]],Pan Jiao, Institute of Anthropology, Minzu University of China. ''The State’s Presence in the Religious Revival in the Liangshan Yi Ethnic Area''. In: ''[https://web.archive.org/web/20140202115753/http://www.ari.nus.edu.sg/showfile.asp?eventfileid=653 Religious Revival in Ethnic Areas of China]''. Asia Research Institute, National University of Singapore, 2011. which incorporates a traditional body of [[ethnomedicine|ethnomedicinal]] knowledge. Furthermore the Yi are fortunate in not having to rely solely upon [[oral tradition]], possessing as they do written records in their own [[Yi script]], dating back at least to the end of the fifteenth centuryMa Xueliang 马学良, ''Han Zang Yu Gailun'' 汉藏语概论 (A General Introduction to Sino-Tibetan Languages) (Beijing, 1991) page 568 and – according to tradition – even farther back to the time of the [[Tang dynasty]].Wu Zili 武自立, ''Chuantong Yiwen'' 传统彝文 (Traditional Yi Script); in ''Zhongguo Shaoshu Minzu Wenzi'' (Beijing, 1991) In the [[Poonch District, Pakistan|Poonch]] region of [[Azad Kashmir]] (Pakistan) a paste of the leaves (or a leaf extract) of ''L. formosa'' (known locally under the name of ''Jummar'') is used as a hair tonic to rid the hair of [[dandruff]] and [[Head louse|lice]]{{citation needed|date=November 2021}} and the same use has been recorded in the [[Kedarnath Wildlife Sanctuary]] of the [[Garhwal Himalaya]] range of [[Uttarakhand]] province, India.{{cite journal |last1=Bhat |first1=Jahangeer A. |last2=Kumar |first2=Munesh |last3=Bussmann |first3=Rainer W. |title=Ecological status and traditional knowledge of medicinal plants in Kedarnath Wildlife Sanctuary of Garhwal Himalaya, India |journal=Journal of Ethnobiology and Ethnomedicine |date=2 January 2013 |volume=9 |issue=1 |pages=1 |doi=10.1186/1746-4269-9-1 |pmid=23281594 |pmc=3560114 |s2cid=6337877 |doi-access=free }} A common name for the plant in 'Chamoli' (= [[Garhwali language|Garhwali]]), spoken in Uttarakhand, is ''Bhenkew''.{{citation needed|date=November 2021}} The [[Monpa people]] of [[Mêdog County]], Southeast Tibet use unspecified plant parts of ''L. formosa'' (known locally by the common name ''pya-min-mon'') to stem blood loss in cases of traumatic [[bleeding]].{{cite journal |last1=Li |first1=Shan |last2=Zhang |first2=Yu |last3=Guo |first3=Yongjie |last4=Yang |first4=Lixin |last5=Wang |first5=Yuhua |title=Monpa, memory, and change: an ethnobotanical study of plant use in Mêdog County, South-east Tibet, China |journal=Journal of Ethnobiology and Ethnomedicine |date=December 2020 |volume=16 |issue=1 |pages=5 |doi=10.1186/s13002-020-0355-7 |pmid=32000826 |pmc=6993401 |doi-access=free }} Shan et al. append to their paper on the ethnobotany of the Monpa a table comparing Monpa plant use for a given species with the reported phytochemical/pharmacological properties of that species as reported in Chinese academic literature and note a good match in the case of ''L. formosa'', although they note further that the plant has been reported elsewhere in China to be used not only to arrest bleeding but also in the treatment of [[bone fracture]]s.Subject database of Chinese plants, medicinal plant database. Institute of Botany, Chinese Academy of Science, Beijing. 2014. http://www.plant.csdb.cn/herb {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211021144523/http://www.plant.csdb.cn/herb |date=2021-10-21 }}. Accessed 9.47 on 2/11/21 Coats gives the common name of the shrub in Nepal as ''nulkuroo'' but does not state the language of that country from which it derives (it is not Nepali). The [[Khaling people]] of the [[Subtropics|subtropical]] lowlands of [[Solukhumbu district]], Nepal use unspecified plant parts of ''L. formosa'' as an [[anthelminthic]]. In his paper on Khaling plant names, Japanese [[missionary]] and ethnographer [[Sueyoshi Toba]] lists the [[Khaling language|Khaling]] name for the plant as ''‘dӕnciki'' and the [[Nepali language|Nepali]] name as ''paDpaDe'', describing the plant itself as 'an aromatic shrub, which sometimes takes parasitic form'.Toba, Sueyoshi, "Plant names in Khaling: a study in ethnobotany and village economy", ''Kailash'' 3(2) pps. 145–169, Kathmandu 1975. This description is curious on two counts, for ''Leycesteria formosa'' – at any rate when grown as an [[Ornamental plant|ornamental shrub]] in Europe – is neither notably aromatic nor a parasite, lacking as it does [[Haustorium|haustoria]] to tap nutrients from a host plant. The latter point, at least, may be explicable by Toba having observed (or heard described by a Khaling informant) ''L. formosa'' growing [[Epiphyte|epiphytically]] upon a tree in a deposit of [[humus]]. The plant is certainly often to be observed growing as a [[lithophyte]] – specifically a chasmophyte – in a minimal [[Substrate (biology)|substrate]], e.g. from bird droppings deposited in rock crevices or in cracks in the [[Mortar (masonry)|mortar]] of old walls. Indeed the plant has been observed growing as a (non-native) epiphyte on the [[tree fern]] ''[[Dicksonia squarrosa]]'' in a survey conducted recently in New Zealand.{{cite journal |last1=Brock |first1=James |last2=Burns |first2=Bruce |title=Patterns of woody plant epiphytism on tree ferns in New Zealand |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/348412042 |journal=New Zealand Journal of Ecology |date=1 January 2021 |volume=45 |issue=1 |page=3433 |doi=10.20417/nzjecol.45.18 |s2cid=231691226 |doi-access=free |hdl=2292/54485 |hdl-access=free }} === Traditional Chinese medicine === In [[Standard Chinese]] ''L. formosa'' is best-known under the common name '''鬼吹簫 (Guĭ chuī xiāo)''' – approximate pronunciation "gwé chwé siaaow"[[Kunming Institute of Botany]], entry "Ghost flute" / ''Leycesteria formosa'' in ''The Complete Database of Higher Plants in China''. Institute of Microbiology, [[Chinese Academy of Sciences]]. [2009-02-24]. (Archived from the original content on 2016-03-05). – meaning '''ghost flute''' (literally ''ghost-blown flute'') / "[[Xiao (flute)|xiao]] of the [[Ghost|spirits]]", although Zhang et al. list also (in translation only) other common names rendered as "[[gun barrel]]", "hollow wood", "wild [[Lupinus|lupine]]" and the more cryptic "golden chicken lock". In the semi-[[Humorism|humoral]] system of [[Traditional Chinese medicine]], as practised in southwest China, the plant is believed to remove excess "dampness" (湿; shī) and "heat" (火; huǒ), to promote blood circulation and to stop bleeding. It is also used to treat (among other diseases/disease concepts) "damp heat [[jaundice]]" (referable possibly to [[hepatitis]]), [[arthritis|arthritic pain]] (notably that caused by [[rheumatoid arthritis]]{{Cite web |title=Leycesteria formosa Wall. |url=https://www-iplant-cn.translate.goog/frps2019/frps/Leycesteria%20formosa?_x_tr_sch=http&_x_tr_sl=zh-CN&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en-GB&_x_tr_pto=op,sc |access-date=2023-08-29 |website= |archive-date=2023-04-21 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230421222237/https://www-iplant-cn.translate.goog/frps2019/frps/Leycesteria%20formosa?_x_tr_sch=http&_x_tr_sl=zh-CN&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en-GB&_x_tr_pto=op,sc |url-status=live }}), [[asthma]], [[irregular menstruation]], [[Urinary tract infection|cystitis]] and bone fracture. ''L. formosa'' is regarded in China as the pre-eminent medicinal species of its genus and has been used there as such for millennia. ==='Ghost flute' and other Chinese common names=== The shrub acquired its picturesque folkloric name of ''ghost flute'' (and also that of 鬼竹子 or Guǐ zhúzi: ''ghost bamboo'') in reference to the eerie piping sounds produced by the broken, hollow stems of the plant when blown upon by the wind.{{Cite web |last= |first= |title=WACA 網路開店｜低成本免抽成，2分鐘打造專屬網路商店 |url=https://www.waca.net/ |access-date=2023-08-29 |website=WACA Store |language=zh-TW |archive-date=2023-08-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230829083637/https://www.waca.net/ |url-status=live }}
Nowadays in the city, the street lights are so bright, even late at night, but it wasn't like that in the countryside when I was a lad. Moonlit nights weren't so bad, but, when you were out walking and there was no moon, it'd be pitch black and you'd start to imagine all sorts of things... When I was a child and I and a few friends would be walking along beside these bushes, they'd make the sound of a flute: I would always think that there really was someone playing the flute, but then I'd look around and there'd be no one there. I'd suddenly feel a bit scared and run away. It got to the point where I'd avoid going near the place where those plants grew: If I so much as caught a glimpse of one, I'd beat a hasty retreat. Maybe, in ancient times, people felt the same way and that's why they gave it the name 'ghost flute', although I expect the herb-gatherers at that time were fond of it and didn't let the sound bother them, because they knew that it was such a good medicinal plant. Later, of course, when I grew up and worked out how the plant made the sound, I realised that there was no reason to be afraid of it any more... it's the stems that make the sound, you see - because they're hollow. If the weather's right and you get a good breeze, you'll hear that rich, melodious sound, just like the blowing of a lot of flutes. and – what with all those pretty little bell flowers dancing around in the wind as well – you'd think the ghosts were blowing on them too...{{Cite web |title=人稱"鬼吹簫"，能發出"簫聲"，兒時看到就走開，藥農卻獨愛它 - 雪花新闻 |url=https://www.xuehua.us/a/5eb91f8186ec4d5748edae11?lang=zh-hk |access-date=2023-08-29 |website=www.xuehua.us |archive-date=2023-05-02 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230502071801/https://www.xuehua.us/a/5eb91f8186ec4d5748edae11?lang=zh-hk |url-status=live }}
In addition to the above, ''L. formosa'' has acquired a wealth of common names in the Chinese language, including:{{Cite web |title=Leycesteria formosa 鬼吹箫 |url=https://www-cfh-ac-cn.translate.goog/(X(1)S(mrhdcjr0jek0v4udvp0rv245))/38615.sp?AspxAutoDetectCookieSupport=1&_x_tr_sch=http&_x_tr_sl=zh-CN&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en-GB&_x_tr_pto=op,sc |access-date=2023-08-29 |website=www-cfh-ac-cn.translate.goog |archive-date=2023-04-21 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230421222237/https://www-cfh-ac-cn.translate.goog/(X(1)S(mrhdcjr0jek0v4udvp0rv245))/38615.sp?AspxAutoDetectCookieSupport=1&_x_tr_sch=http&_x_tr_sl=zh-CN&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en-GB&_x_tr_pto=op,sc |url-status=live }} * 风吹箫 (Fēng chuī xiāo): Wind(-blown) flute * 夜吹箫 (Yè chuī xiāo): Night(-blowing) flute * 大追风 (Dà zhuī fēng): Big chase wind * 炮筒花 (Pào tǒng huā): Gun barrel flower * 炮竹筒 (Pào zhútǒng): Firecracker (Pào 'gun' + zhútǒng 'bamboo tube') * 炮仗筒 (Pàozhang tǒng): Firecracker (Pàozhang 'gun battle' + tǒng 'tube') * 火炮花 (Huǒpào huā): Artillery flower * 金鸡一把锁 (Jīnjī yī bǎ suǒ): Golden rooster lock * 空心木 (Kōngxīn mù): Hollow wood * 空心草 (Kōngxīn cǎo): Hollow grass * 大笔杆草 (Dà bǐgǎn cǎo): Big pen grass/Big-stalked grass * 来色木 (Lái shǎi mù): (Come) colour wood * 大木比替力 (Dà mù bǐ tì lì): Big wood that is a substitute for strength * 鬼竹子 (Guǐ zhúzi): Ghost bamboo * 梅叶竹 (Méi yè zhú): Plum-leaved bamboo * 野芦柴 (Yě Lú chái): Wild reed firewood * 磨倮子 (Mó luǒ zi): Grinding naked seed * 猴橘子 (Hóu júzi): Monkey orange{{citation needed|date=October 2022}} These names refer mostly to the tubular ([[Fistula#Botany|fistular]]) form of the stems, their similarity to those of bamboos and their suitability for wind instruments – as suggested by their natural tendency to whistle eerily in the wind. Those referring to (again, tubular) guns and fireworks indicate that the jointed stems of the plant explode (crack / pop) when burnt, like those of bamboo (the popping stems of which the first fireworks were manufactured to mimic{{cite book|first=Joseph|last=Needham|year=1986|publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]]|title=Science and Civilisation in China, Volume 5: Chemistry and Chemical Technology, Part 7: Military Technology: The Gunpowder Epic|isbn=0-521-30358-3|page=140}}). Only one common name (Hóu júzi, 'Monkey orange') references the shrub's edible berries, and does so in a somewhat disparaging manner. The curious name Jīnjī yī bǎ suǒ, translating as 'Golden rooster lock', suggests that the plant was thought to relate in some way to the good luck / wealth-bringing symbol of the golden cockerel.Images of wealth-bringing symbol the golden cockerel https://wantubizhi.com/pic/金鸡吉祥图片/ {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250123144506/https://wantubizhi.com/pic/%E9%87%91%E9%B8%A1%E5%90%89%E7%A5%A5%E5%9B%BE%E7%89%87/ |date=2025-01-23 }} Retrieved at 20.02 on Wednesday 5/1/22. == Other uses == The hollow canes produced by ''L. formosa'' have been used in India to make [[whistle]]s and flutes.Gupta, B.L. ''Forest Flora of Chakrata, Dehra Dun and Saharanpur'' pub. Forest Research Institute Press 1945Gamble, J.S. ''A Manual of Indian Timbers'', pub. Bishen Singh Mahendra Pal Singh 1972 Other uses of the plant in North India (states [[Assam]], [[Himachal Pradesh]], [[Jammu and Kashmir (union territory)]], [[Ladakh]] and [[Sikkim]]) are as a [[green manure]] and as [[firewood]].{{Cite web |title=Leycesteria formosa Wall. {{!}} Species |url=https://indiabiodiversity.org/species/show/230235 |access-date=2023-08-29 |website=India Biodiversity Portal |language=en}}Hooker, J. D., (1880) Flora of British India. Reprint by Bishen Singh Mahendra Pal Singh, Publishers, Dehra Dun. 3: 16. == Animal toxicity == While many sources assert that ''L. formosa'' is not toxic, there have been associated deaths of cattle reported in New Zealand and Australia, where the plant is a rampant weed, and thus the plant is best considered suspect until more conclusive evidence comes to light. Leaves and unripe berries are likely to have been the plant parts browsed. Though this plant is often confused with [[Tutu (plant)|Tutu]] a plant with poisonous seeds in [[New Zealand|Aotearoa]], this plant shares an almost identical habitat, leaf shape, hollow stems, and a deep connection with traditional health practices called [[rongoā]].{{Cite web |title=Browse and Search the Tortoise Table Plant Database |url=https://www.thetortoisetable.org.uk/plant-database/viewplants/?plant=484&c=4#.YYWpBC3fVvJ |access-date=2023-08-29 |website=www.thetortoisetable.org.uk |archive-date=2023-04-21 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230421220737/https://www.thetortoisetable.org.uk/plant-database/viewplants/?plant=484&c=4#.YYWpBC3fVvJ |url-status=live }}Hill F, Scotland T, Grant I, "Deaths in cattle associated with Leycesteria formosa (Himalayan honeysuckle) consumption" ''Society of Sheep and Beef Cattle Veterinarians Newsletter'', Issue 37, Jun 2010 Publisher: The society of Sheep and Beef Cattle Veterinarians of the New Zealand Veterinary Association http://www.sciquest.org.nz/node/142297 {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211105225904/http://www.sciquest.org.nz/node/142297 |date=2021-11-05 }} Retrieved at 22.58 on Friday 5/11/21. == Chemistry == ''Leycesteria formosa'' has yielded [[coumarin]]s, monomeric [[flavonoids]] and the two [[biflavonoid]] compounds [[amentoflavone]] (3'–8" biapigenin) and its 4"'methyl derivative [[podocarpusflavone A]]. Amentoflavone and, to some extent, podocarpusflavone A are good [[cyclic adenosine monophosphate|cAMP]] [[phosphodiesterase-4 inhibitor]]s. In the light of these findings ''L. formosa'' may be considered of potential interest in the treatment of [[dermatitis]]. Prior to the isolation of amentoflavone from ''Leycesteria'', the only genera of Caprifoliaceae in which the compound was known to occur were ''[[Viburnum]]'' and ''[[Lonicera]]''.{{cite journal |last1=Lobstein |first1=A |last2=Yepes |first2=Y |last3=Um |first3=BH |last4=Weniger |first4=B |last5=Lugnier |first5=C |last6=Anton |first6=R |title=Bioactive compounds from Leycesteria formosa |journal=Die Pharmazie |date=June 2002 |volume=57 |issue=6 |pages=431–432 |id={{INIST|13719925}} |pmid=12116886 }} (Note: the genus ''Viburnum'' is now placed, not in Caprifoliaceae, but in the related family [[Viburnaceae]]). The leaves of ''L. formosa'' have been found to contain [[leucoanthocyanins]],''A Comparative Phytochemical Study of Caprifoliaceae'' Doctoral Thesis of Charles William Glennie, The University of British Columbia, submitted November 1969, p.17. https://open.library.ubc.ca/media/download/pdf/831/1.0102080/1 {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221007224944/https://open.library.ubc.ca/media/download/pdf/831/1.0102080/1 |date=2022-10-07 }} Retrieved at 13.39 on Friday 5/11/21. while the wood contains the fluorescent [[lactone]] [[aesculetin]]. ==Gallery== File:Leycesteria formosa (Planche de Wallich).jpg|The misleadingly "highly coloured" plate 120 from [[Nathaniel Wallich]]'s ''Plantae asiaticae rariores'', published London 1830 File:Leycesteria Formosa Paxton pre.
